---
title: "Reporting"
---


Many journals now require a reporting checklist with a qualitative
submission. Filling one in from memory at the end is how the numbers in a
methods section drift away from what the analysis actually did. These two
functions produce the checklist with the derivable parts already answered
from your data.

## COREQ

Thirty-two items across research team, study design, and analysis and
findings, aimed at interviews and focus groups.

```python
cq = qdapy.coreq(fragments = frag, history = history, codebook = codebook)
cq[cq["filled"]][["item", "name", "answer"]]
print(qdapy.coreq_markdown(cq))
```

Six items come out of the data: how many documents, how many coders, how
large the code system, whether saturation was reached, what software was
used, and how many quotable fragments there are. The remaining twenty-six are
marked *To be completed*, which is the other half of the point: the gaps are
visible instead of forgotten.

::: {.callout-warning title="COREQ never asks about agreement"}

There is no item for intercoder reliability. If you computed it, it
belongs in your answer to item 24 or 25, and the checklist will not
prompt you.
:::

## SRQR

Twenty-one standards covering the whole report rather than interviews
specifically. Reach for it when your material is not interview transcripts,
or when the journal names it.

```python
sq = qdapy.srqr(fragments = frag, history = history)
print(qdapy.srqr_markdown(sq))
```

Unlike COREQ, SRQR **does** have a home for the agreement figure: standard
S15, techniques to enhance trustworthiness, names the audit trail explicitly,
and a coding log is one. If both checklists are acceptable to your journal
and you have reliability figures to report, that is a reason to prefer SRQR.

## What is filled, and what is not

Only what the exports genuinely determine. Nothing here writes your
methodological rationale, and nothing guesses. Where an item needs a file you
did not pass, it stays empty rather than being answered from a default:
saturation needs the history export, the coding tree needs the codebook.

The checklist items are reproduced verbatim from the published tables. A
checklist paraphrased is one a reviewer cannot match against the original,
which defeats the purpose of having a standard.

## Both, in one go

Nothing stops you generating both and keeping whichever the journal asks for:

```python
open("coreq.md", "w").write(qdapy.coreq_markdown(qdapy.coreq(frag, history)))
open("srqr.md", "w").write(qdapy.srqr_markdown(qdapy.srqr(frag, history)))
```
